chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Bid-Ask Spread: What It Is Made Of

lessons.title: Why Nifty Options Trade Tighter Than a Small-Cap Stock's Spread

body.text: A Nifty weekly option and a thinly traded small-cap stock option are priced by the exact same three-part formula. What differs is not the formula, it is how small or large each of its three inputs is allowed to become, and by how much competition is left to squeeze them further.

children.text: Spread equals order processing cost plus inventory holding cost plus adverse selection cost, for every instrument on NSE without exception. A Nifty 50 index weekly option and a mid-month option on a rarely traded small-cap are both priced by that same equation. The reason one routinely trades one to two ticks wide and the other can sit twenty ticks wide or wider is that every single term on the right-hand side of that equation is smaller for the index option, and a fourth force, competition among market makers, has far more room to squeeze what is left.
Order Processing: Fixed Costs Spread Over Enormous Volume

Technology, connectivity, compliance, and per-trade exchange charges cost roughly the same whether a market maker quotes a contract that trades a handful of times a day or one that trades tens of thousands of times. Nifty options are, by contract volume, among the most actively traded derivatives products globally, so that largely fixed cost gets divided across an enormous number of trades, making the order processing charge embedded in each individual quote tiny. The same fixed cost, spread over a small-cap option's handful of daily trades, has to be recovered from far fewer trades, so each one has to carry a larger slice of it.
Inventory: Thick, Two-Sided Flow Means Fast Offload

Recall from Chapter 1 that inventory holding cost grows with how long a market maker expects to sit on a position before offloading it. On a Nifty option, buy and sell orders arrive constantly from both directions, so a market maker that just bought from one trader can typically sell that same position back to a different trader within seconds. On an illiquid small-cap option, the next order on the opposite side might not show up for minutes or hours, so a resulting position sits exposed to price risk for far longer, and the spread has to be wide enough to compensate for that extended holding period.

body.label: Holding Time Drives the Inventory Component
body.context: A market maker on a liquid Nifty option can often expect an offsetting order within seconds. On a thin small-cap option, the same market maker may hold a position for hours before another trader shows up on the opposite side, multiplying the inventory risk it has to price into its quote.

children.text: Adverse Selection: Diversification Dilutes the Informed Trader's Edge

Someone with genuine advance knowledge about a single company's results can trade that company's stock options profitably on that information alone, and a market maker on the other side has no diversification to hide behind: the entire loss lands on one name. The same piece of information barely moves Nifty at all, since the index is an average across fifty constituent stocks, so even a trader who somehow knew one company's results in advance gets very little edge from trading the index option on it. This is precisely why adverse selection cost is structurally smaller for an index product than for a single stock: the information that actually exists in the market is diluted across fifty names before it reaches the index level.

body.text: This lesson describes information asymmetry as a market microstructure concept, not as a trading tactic. Trading on genuine unpublished price-sensitive information about a specific company is insider trading, prohibited under SEBI's Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations, 2015, regardless of which instrument, stock or derivative, it is expressed through.

children.text: Even after all three cost components shrink, there is a final force at work: a liquid Nifty option is quoted by dozens of proprietary trading desks and market participants competing directly against each other, none of whom needs an exchange incentive to bother showing up. Any one of them quoting a wider spread than it needs to simply loses order flow to a competitor quoting tighter. An illiquid stock option, by contrast, may have only the exchange's specifically appointed Liquidity Enhancement Scheme market maker from Chapter 1 providing a meaningful two-way quote at all, with little to no competitive pressure forcing that spread down any further than the scheme's own maximum ceiling requires.

body.caption: Why the same spread formula produces very different numbers

cells: Fixed costs spread across enormous trade volume
Same fixed costs spread across very few trades
Offsetting orders typically arrive within seconds
Offsetting orders may take minutes to hours to arrive
Company-specific information is diluted across 50 constituents
Company-specific information lands on a single name in full
Many market makers competing without needing an exchange incentive
Often just one LES-appointed market maker, with limited competitive pressure

body.text: None of these four drivers is unique to options. The same logic explains why Nifty and Bank Nifty futures trade tighter than a small-cap stock's own shares, and why the most liquid part of any market, index or single-name, is always the part with the most volume, the fastest offload, the most diluted information, and the most competing quotes.

body.title: Diagnosing a Wide Spread
body.scenario: A quant researcher compares two contracts on the same day: a Nifty 50 ATM weekly call trading at a 1-tick spread with heavy volume throughout the session, and a monthly call option on a small-cap stock that has traded only six times all day, currently quoted at a spread twenty times as wide.
body.prompt: Using the four drivers from this lesson, explain the small-cap option's wide spread. Which driver would you expect to matter least here, order processing or the other three?
body.modelAnswer: The small-cap option's spread is wide because of a combination of higher inventory holding cost, since offsetting orders arrive rarely and a resulting position may sit exposed for a long time, higher adverse selection cost, since any real information about this single company lands on this one option rather than being diluted across an index, and weak competitive pressure, since it is likely quoted by only one market maker with little competition forcing the spread tighter. Order processing cost, while technically also higher per trade here due to low volume, is usually the least important driver of the size of the gap between the two contracts, since fixed operating costs are a smaller share of the total spread compared to the much larger swings in inventory and adverse selection risk between a liquid index option and an illiquid single stock option.

body.title: Index vs Single Stock
body.question: Why does genuine company-specific information create a smaller adverse selection cost for a Nifty index option than for that company's own stock option?
options: Because index options have lower exchange transaction charges
Because the information's effect on the index is diluted across all the index's constituent stocks
Because index options do not allow market makers to lose money on adverse selection
Because index options have wider tick sizes than stock options
body.explanation: A single company's news moves that company's own stock, and its options, in full. The same news moves an index only by that company's small weight within it, since the index averages across all its constituents. That dilution is exactly why adverse selection cost, the cost of trading against someone with real information, is structurally lower for index products than for single-stock products.

points: The same three-part spread formula applies to every NSE instrument; what differs between Nifty options and illiquid stock options is the size of each component
Order processing cost per trade is lower for Nifty options because fixed costs are spread over far higher volume
Inventory holding cost is lower for Nifty options because offsetting order flow arrives quickly, often within seconds, rather than after minutes or hours
Adverse selection cost is structurally lower for an index option because single-company information is diluted across all of the index's constituents
Competition among many market makers on liquid Nifty options compresses spreads further than the limited competition typical of an LES-appointed single market maker on an illiquid contract
Trading on genuine unpublished company information is insider trading under SEBI's Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations, 2015, regardless of the instrument used to express it
